title: Aash-e anar
subtitle: Persian pomegranate and herb soup
excerpt: Aash-e anar is a Persian sweet-sour soup made with pomegranate juice, yellow split peas, and a generous quantity of fresh herbs. Finished with pomegranate seeds and walnuts, it is vibrant in colour and flavour. It is a Nowruz soup, associated with the Persian New Year and the return of spring.
sourceNotes: A Persian ash (thick soup) made with pomegranate. Anar means pomegranate in Persian. The soup is traditionally made at Nowruz and at the winter solstice festival Yalda Night.

recipe.freezeNotes: Not recommended; the herbs lose their colour and the pomegranate juice changes flavour on freezing.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keeps for 2 days in the fridge. Add the fresh pomegranate seeds and walnuts just before serving.

content.text: Aash-e anar is beautiful to look at: a deep garnet soup scattered with fresh pomegranate seeds and toasted walnuts. The colour comes from pomegranate juice, which also gives the soup its defining quality: a tartness that is balanced by the richness of the peas and the body of the herbs.
The soup is in the ash family, which means it is thick and satisfying rather than clear and delicate. Yellow split peas give it body and a pleasant earthiness that carries the pomegranate well.
Use the best pomegranate juice you can find. Fresh-pressed or cold-pressed versions give a brighter, sharper result than long-life juice from a carton.

items.prepNote: as juice; use cold-pressed bottled pomegranate juice or juice 3 to 4 fresh pomegranates

content.text: Heat the oil in a large saucepan over medium heat. Add the onion and cook for 8 minutes until golden. Add the turmeric, then the split peas and stock. Bring to the boil, reduce to a simmer, and cook for 30 minutes until the peas are completely soft.

Pour in the pomegranate juice. Add the parsley, mint, and spinach. Stir in the salt and sugar. Simmer for 15 more minutes until the herbs are cooked and the soup has taken on a deep pink-red colour. Taste and adjust the balance of sweet and sour with extra sugar or pomegranate juice.
Ladle into deep bowls. Scatter pomegranate seeds and toasted walnuts over each serving. Add the fried dried mint on top if using.

rows.cause: Pomegranate juice more acidic than expected
rows.fix: Add sugar one teaspoon at a time and stir; the balance should be sweet-sour, not sharp.

rows.symptom: Split peas not soft at 30 minutes
rows.fix: Continue simmering for another 15 to 20 minutes. Very old peas can take considerably longer.

rows.cause: Long-life boxed juice or juice added too early
rows.fix: Use fresh or cold-pressed pomegranate juice and add it later in the cooking process.

content.text: Add a handful of rice or pearl barley to the soup with the split peas for extra body. Some versions include meatballs; small lamb or beef meatballs are added to the pot for the last 20 minutes of cooking.
The soup base can be made 2 days ahead and refrigerated. Reheat gently and scatter the fresh pomegranate and walnuts immediately before serving; they lose their texture if added during storage.

Aash-e anar is closely associated with Nowruz and with Yalda Night, the winter solstice celebration. Pomegranate is a symbol of life in Persian culture, and its colour and flavour run through many festival dishes. The soup appears in Persian households on these occasions and is one of the most distinctive dishes in the Iranian festive calendar.
